displayQuote: Nothing strengthens authority so much as silence

meta.title: Who really said "Nothing strengthens authority so much as silence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Leonardo da Vinci. The line is Charles de Gaulle, from his 1931 essay “Du Prestige” (book: Le Fil de l’épée, 1932). The da Vinci credit first appeared in 2004.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing strengthens authority so much as silence'?
meta.ogDescription: Not da Vinci — Charles de Gaulle wrote it in 1931 (“Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence”). The English wording is a loose translation.

answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — actually Charles de Gaulle
answer.authorDates: 1890–1970 · French general & President of the Fifth Republic
answer.sourceLine: De Gaulle wrote this in his 1931 essay “Du Prestige” in the ‘Revue Militaire Française,’ later collected in his book ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (1932): “Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence.” The popular English “strengthens” wording is one of several loose translations of that line. There is no evidence Leonardo da Vinci — who died in 1519 — ever wrote it; the da Vinci credit first surfaced only in 2004.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: “Du Prestige” (1931); collected in ‘Le Fil de l’épée’
English ‘The Edge of the Sword,’ tr. Gerard Hopkins, 1960

source.excerpt: Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence, splendeur des forts et refuge des faibles, pudeur des orgueilleux et fierté des humbles, prudence des sages et esprit des sots.
trail: Charles de Gaulle, 1931. Quote Investigator traces the line to de Gaulle’s essay “Du Prestige” in the ‘Revue Militaire Française,’ collected the next year in ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (1932): “Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence” ↗.

The French is on record. Wikiquote’s de Gaulle page carries the original — “Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence, splendeur des forts et refuge des faibles” ↗ — sourced to ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (1932).

The da Vinci credit is late and baseless. Per Quote Investigator, Leonardo — who died in 1519 — was first tied to the line only in 2004, in a Washington Post letter ↗, with quote sites like Goodreads ↗ spreading it since.
source.excerptNote: De Gaulle’s original French. Gerard Hopkins’s 1960 authorized translation renders the opening as “Nothing more enhances authority than silence” — the widely shared “strengthens authority so much as silence” is a looser, unattributed rendering of the same sentence.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of Charles de Gaulle / French publisher (Berger-Levrault, later Plon); English translation © Gerard Hopkins / Faber & Faber (1960)
source.rightsNote: The line comes from de Gaulle’s ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (first published 1931–1932), well after 1931, so both the French original and Gerard Hopkins’s 1960 English translation remain in copyright in the United States. The exact popular “strengthens” wording is an unattributed variant translation, but it derives directly from that copyrighted work, so no public-domain claim is safe.

author.name: Charles de Gaulle
author.heading: About Charles de Gaulle
author.metaLine: 1890–1970 · French general, leader of Free France & President of the Fifth Republic
author.bio: Charles de Gaulle was a French army officer and statesman who led the Free French forces against Nazi Germany and later founded the Fifth Republic, serving as President from 1959 to 1969. Before the war he was a military theorist whose 1932 book Le Fil de l’épée (The Edge of the Sword) laid out his thinking on leadership, character and command — including the meditation on silence that later drifted onto Leonardo da Vinci.

misattribution.heading: How da Vinci got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine de Gaulle line that migrated onto Leonardo da Vinci — one of the internet’s biggest magnets for orphaned aphorisms — centuries after his death.

items.why: De Gaulle wrote “Rien ne rehausse l’autorité mieux que le silence” in his 1931 essay “Du Prestige,” collected in ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (1932), per Quote Investigator ↗.
Da Vinci died in 1519 and left no such line. Quote Investigator found the ascription surfacing only in 2004 ↗, then spreading through quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ and BrainyQuote.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are Charles de Gaulle’s, from ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ (1932); the English “Nothing strengthens authority so much as silence” is a loose translation, and the Leonardo da Vinci credit is a 21st-century error ↗.

context.heading: Why it fits de Gaulle
lead: De Gaulle wrote ‘Le Fil de l’épée’ as a study of military leadership and the authority of command. The full sentence is a small prose-poem on silence — “splendour of the strong and refuge of the weak” — and reads as the credo of a man who would later cultivate an almost oracular reserve as a wartime leader and head of state.

Stripped of its French cadence and its author, the opening clause became a generic leadership maxim, easily reassigned to a more universally ‘quotable’ genius. Leonardo da Vinci — endlessly credited with feel-good aphorisms he never wrote — was the natural magnet.
context.pull: “Nothing more enhances authority than silence” — the crowning virtue of the strong, in de Gaulle’s own book on command.
